extracted.intended_audience: authors, copyeditors, proofreaders, librarians, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive style rules for capitalization, italics, quotations, and spelling intended to guide editors and authors in preparing printed/professional text according to the University of Chicago Press Manual of Style conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 42. Capitalization of foreign titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles, in addition to capitalizing the first word, follow specified language-specific rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: a) Latin: capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived therefrom (e.g., De amicitia, Bellum Gallicum). b) French, Italian, Spanish, Swedish, Norwegian: capitalize proper nouns but not adjectives derived therefrom (e.g., Histoire de la litterature francaise). c) German and Danish: capitalize all nouns but not adjectives, except German adjectives derived from names of persons (e.g., Geschichte des deutschen Feudalwesens; but: die Homerische Frage). d) Dutch: capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns (e.g., Geschiedenis der Nederlandsche Taal).

rubrics_metrics.name: 43. Treatment of definite article in periodical/newspaper titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title when mentioning newspapers, magazines, and similar publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Chicago Tribune, the School Review, the Annual Register of the University of Chicago.

rubrics_metrics.name: 44. Titles of ancient manuscripts (MS/MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts; abbreviate as MS (singular) and MSS (plural).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Codex Bernensis, Cod. Canonicianus. (See also rule 60.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 45. Capitalization in hyphenated compound titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with the main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds, but do not capitalize components when other than nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Twentieth-Century Progress," "The Economy of High-Speed Trains." Do not capitalize non-noun components. In side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper nouns (see rules 56 and 172). Examples: Fifty-first Street, "Lives of Well-known Authors," "World-Dominion of English-speaking Peoples."

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Capitalization of scientific (Latin) names of higher taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological matter, capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera, but not their English derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cotylosauria (but: cotylosaurs); Felidae (but: felids); Carnivora (but: carnivores). Also capitalize species names if derived from names of persons or from generic names in botanical/zoological matter; species names are never capitalized in geological and medical matter. Examples: Felis leo, Cocos nucifera, Rosa Carolina, Parkinsonia Torreyana, Styrax californica; but geological example: Pterygomatopus schmidti, Conodectus favosus. (See rule 71.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Capitalization of names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro (in its ethnic sense), Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Capitalization in astronomical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of planetary bodies, stars, and groups of stars (but not common words like 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' 'stars'); capitalize designations of celestial objects in well-known catalogues and Flamsteed numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Saturn, Ursa Major, the Milky Way, the Great Bear; M 13 (Messier), Bond 619, N.G.C. 6165, B.D.-180487i; 85 Pegasi, Lalande 5761.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. Capitalization of university divisions and officers (University of Chicago examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago in all official work dealing with its administration or curricula; provide parenthetical shortened forms where indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (the University), the School of Education (the School), University Extension Division (but: the division), Department of Anthropology (also: the Department); the Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board), the Senate, the Council, University College (also: the College); Dean of the Faculties (also: the Faculty); the President, the Recorder, Professor of Physics, Assistant in Chemistry, Fellow, Scholar; Van Husen Scholarship (but: the scholarship). Also usage for course/session names: courses in Political Economy, Autumn Quarter (but: a quarter), First Term (but: two terms; major, minor).

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Use of caps and small caps for letter date/salutatory/signature lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Set town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles, in caps and small caps with specified indentation and placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and layout: CHICAGO, ILL., January 1, 1911 (set to the right, one em indent, preferably smaller type); MY DEAR MR. SMITH: (set flush, followed by a colon, same type as body, separate line). Signatures and institutional names set to the right or left with specified indention and type sizes; examples: CHARLES W. SCOTT; HARVARD UNIVERSITY CAMBRIDGE, MASS. June 7, 1911 (date left, two ems' indention, smaller type). Each line of address in caps and small caps, centered on the one preceding; date in caps and lower case, likewise centered.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Capitals in resolutions, notes, and constitutions/by-laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'WHEREAS' in resolutions; 'NOTE' in notes (not footnotes) followed by a period and a dash; 'SECTION' introducing paragraphs in constitutions/by-laws, followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usage examples: NOTE. — It should be noticed that ... SECTION 1. This association shall be styled ... Usual practice is to abbreviate 'section' after the first use: SECTION 1. ... SEC. 2. The object of the association ....

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Small capitals for time era abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M./P.M. and B.C./A.D. in small capitals without spaces between letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use lower-case initial letters for commonized proper names and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small (lower-case) initial letter for words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives whose origin has become obscured; also generally for verbs derived from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, anglicize, macadamize, paris green.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lower-case for minor subdivisions in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case for minor subdivisions and their abbreviations in literary references: chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; with abbreviations chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (See rules 37, 110, and 237.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Lower-case for units of measurement abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initials for common units of measurement abbreviations: h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second; lb.=pound, oz.=ounce; yd.=yard, ft.=foot; etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed in rule: h., min., sec., lb., oz., yd., ft., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Capitalization in side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: In side-heads (subheadings), capitalize only the first word and proper names (see rules 172 and 280).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also rule 45 for hyphenated compounds and rule 172 for further side-head guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Capitalize first word of a quotation connected to the preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a quotation which, through a conjunction or otherwise, is immediately connected with what precedes, even if such word begins a sentence in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Use of italics for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which it is desired to lend emphasis, importance, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "This was, however, not the case"; "It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes."

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italics for foreign words/phrases not incorporated into English and short foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text and not incorporated into English; also usually single sentences or brief passages not long enough to set in reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "the Darwinian Weltanschauung"; "Napoleon's coup d'etat"; "De gustibus non est disputandum". Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names, names of foreign institutions/places whose English use requires roman type, or everyday words sufficiently anglicized even if retaining accents (examples follow in the list of many foreign words).

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italics for titles of publications (books, pamphlets, periodicals, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of publications — books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, and single long poems), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, periodicals — and the name of a journal appearing in itself; include city if integral to the name for newspapers/periodicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer-Night's Dream; Idylls of the King; Paradise Lost; the Modern Language Review; the Chicago Tribune; Report of the United States Commissioner of Education. Note: Botanical Gazette uses italics for such titles in text only; in footnotes, roman, and prints its own name in caps and small caps. Rule may be departed from in lengthy bibliographical lists, tables, or where italics would be excessive. Books of the Bible and titles of ancient manuscripts should be set in roman type; symbols used to designate manuscripts set in roman (see rules 31 and 44).

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italics for certain words/abbreviations in literary and legal references
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ad loc., circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, sc., supra, s.v., vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But do not italicize cf., e.g., i.e., v. or vs. (unless ambiguity would result), viz., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Italics for cross-reference words in indexes/errata lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize the words See and See also in an index or similar compilation when used for cross-references, and the words for and read in lists of errata to separate them from incorrect and correct readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: See also Sociology; for levee read levee.

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Italics for names of parties in legal citations and titles of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize the names of plaintiff and defendant in citations of legal causes; also titles of proceedings containing prefixes such as in re, ex parte, in the matter of, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Italics/capitalization for address lines and primary address lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Set address lines in speeches, reports, etc., and primary address lines in letters flush in a separate line, with nouns capitalized; these may be set in italics as prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen: Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill. DEAR SIR: I take pleasure in announcing ...

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Formatting of position/title in signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name should be placed according to length: one-word titles run into same line; more than one word (no longer than the name) center first letter under the name line and indent one em on the right; if longer than the name, center the name over the second line and set the title flush. Rules subject to special-case exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ARTHUR P. MAGUIRE, Secretary; Yours very truly, CARTER H. HARRISON Mayor of Chicago; CHARLES M. GAYLEY Professor of English Language and Literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Use of letters for subdivisions and fractional indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc., to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if 'run in'); use a, b, c, etc. affixed to verse/page numbers to denote fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:3a.

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Letters to designate unknown quantities in technical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ac+bc=c(a+b)', the lines ad and AD; the nth power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Letters in legends referring to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, use letters in legends or in the text referring to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).'

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. References to particular letters spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to particular letters, reference them in text as 'the letter u, a small v, a capital S.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use context-appropriate phrasing when referring to specific glyphs or letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. Abbreviations for old currency shillings and pence following numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use s. and d. (= shillings and pence) following numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 35s. 6d. (See rule 270.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Italics for generic + species Latin names in zoological/geological/paleontological matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter, italicize scientific (Latin) names of genera and species when used together, with the generic name in nominative singular; italicize genera when used alone. In medical matter, general practice is to print such names in roman, avoiding italics altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodectes favosus, Phyteuma Halleri. Genera/species examples: Acer saccharum, Basidiobolus, Alternaria, Erythrosuchus. See rules 46 and 48. Also notes about astronomical usages (Fraunhofer letters, Baeyer's letters) and a subsequent statement: modern practice is to avoid italics for certain symbol/letter conventions (see follow-up guidance in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: 71a. Astronomical italicization exceptions and catalogue initials
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical/astrophysical matter: (a) lower-case letters designating Fraunhofer lines are italicized; (b) lower-case letters used by Baeyer for stars when Greek letters exhausted are italicized; (c) initials used as titles of catalogues (as such) should be italicized when not designating a particular object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a, b, g, h; / Tauri, u Herculis; catalogue initials italicized: B.D., N.G.C. Also, modern practice: do not use italics for symbols of chemical elements, Fraunhofer capital letters for spectral lines, letters designating spectral types, or combined H with Greek letters for hydrogen lines (see last subsections under rule 71).

rubrics_metrics.name: 71b. Modern practice to avoid italics for certain technical symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use italics for: (a) symbols for chemical elements (H, Ca, Ti); (b) Fraunhofer capital letters for spectral lines (A-H, K); (c) letters designating spectral types (A5, B4, Mb); (d) capital H combined with Greek letters for hydrogen lines (Ha, Hβ, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This instruction follows rule 71's discussion on usages where italics are no longer recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. Use of 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions, use the word 'Resolved' (see rule 39).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short directive; cross-reference to earlier rule on style for resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Use of 'Continued' after headlines or 'To be continued'
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, use the word 'Continued'; and 'To be continued' at the end of articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY— Continued; [To be continued]. See rule 179 for continuation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Use quotation marks (roman-quote) for run-in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put between quotation marks (and in roman type) citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 85 for when to set quoted matter in smaller type instead of using quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Quotation marks for consecutive quotations without intervening original matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for quotations from different authors, or from different works by the same author, following each other uninterrupted by intervening original matter or by references to sources (other than a footnote figure), even if reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced quotations exceptions noted in rules 85-87.

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Quotation marks for words/phrases accompanied by definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for a word or phrase accompanied by its definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-folio' means a page-number at the foot of the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. Quotation marks for unusual/technical/ironical words or phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for unusual, technical, ironical, etc., words or phrases in the text, whether or not accompanied by a word like 'so-called.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; She was wearing a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk; He was elected 'master of the rolls'; This so-called 'man of affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Quotation marks for translations inserted into text
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, place the English equivalent of a foreign word/phrase/passage in quotation marks when inserted into the English text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen, Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Quotation marks to draw attention to particular words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to single out or direct attention to particular words or phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Quotation marks for titles of book series
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of book series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters Series'; 'International Critical Commentary'; the series 'Handbooks of Ethics and Religion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. Quotation marks for titles of shorter poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.' (See rule 60 for longer poems printed separately.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions and other shorter works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters) of publications; titles of papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Beginnings of the Science of Political Economy, Vol. I, 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; articles 'Cross,' 'Crucifixion,' and 'Crusade' in Hastings' Dictionary of the Bible; the lecture subject 'Japan — Its Past, Present, and Future'; the toast 'Our Canadian Visitor'; The king's motto is 'For God and My Country.' Note: Botanical Gazette in footnotes does not use quotation marks for such titles. References to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index, etc., of a specific work should be set with capitals without quotation marks: Preface, p. iii; but quoted usages for certain commentary: 'The Introduction contains ...' etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Set names of ships in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. Quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. Set long quotations in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily set all prose extracts that will make five or more lines in smaller type, and all poetry citations of two lines or more, in smaller type rather than run them into the text. An isolated prose quotation may be run into the text if organically related to the argument; short lines adjacent to longer extracts set in smaller type may be reduced for uniform appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is guidance on when to set quoted matter as block/shortened type rather than inline quotations. See rules 86-87 for reduction sizes and punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Reduction sizes for quoted matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce type sizes for quotations according to a mapping: from n-pt. and 20-pt. to g-pt., from 12-pt. to 8-pt., from 8-pt. to 6-pt. (see rule 252).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for typographic reduction; see rule 252 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Punctuation and quotation marks for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations should not have quotation marks, except in cases noted in rule 75; nor should quotation marks, as a rule, be used in connection with italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: cases discussed in rule 75 (consecutive quotations) and other specific circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when indicating omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when it otherwise would not be clear that it stands for an omitted part of the matter quoted; perfect clarity in each individual case is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate inclusion/exclusion: when 'etc.' is part of the title abbreviation versus when 'etc.' indicates omitted part of a quotation, placement relative to quotation marks may differ to preserve meaning and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Repeat opening quotation marks for multi-paragraph quoted prose
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoted prose is broken into paragraphs, repeat the opening quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the reader recognizes the entire block as a single quotation spanning paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. 'Clearing' quotation marks when alignment is desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment is desired, set quotation marks 'cleared'—i.e., projecting beyond the line of alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows opening quotation mark projecting to align quote text: "Keep away from dirtiness — keep away from mess. Don't get into doin' things rather-more-or-less ! "

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Use double quotation marks for primary quotations, single for nested
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations; for a quotation within a quotation, use single marks; alternate back to double for a third level, single for a fourth, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show nested quotations from Rossetti's Life of Keats with alternating double/single marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: 92. Spell out most religious, civil, and military titles preceding the name; abbreviate certain common ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all religious, civil, and military titles of honor and respect and forms of address preceding the name, except commonly abbreviated forms (Mr., Messrs., Mrs., M., MM., Mme, Mile, Dr., Rev., Hon., St.). Do not set Rev. or Hon. except in quotations and correspondence; Esq. following the name should likewise be abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule with exceptions for quotations/correspondence; guidance on customary abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Spell out Christian names and 'von' in ordinary text
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Christian names (George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviating (not: Geo., Chas., Jno.), except where abbreviated form appears in quoted matter or original signatures; also spell out 'von' as part of a person's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abbreviations only in quoted material or signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Spell out numbers of less than three digits in ordinary reading matter (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading matter, spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless of a statistical or technical character, or occurring in groups of six or more following each other in close succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' 'a fifty-yard dash'; exceptions: use figures for decimals, degrees, dimensions, distances, enumerations, money, percentages, weights, and similar technical/statistical matter (10°, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, 100 bushels, 9 per cent, 45 pounds, $1,000). Also, treat numbers in connected groups alike; if the largest has three or more digits, use figures for all (see rule 96).

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Spell out round numbers (approximate figures) in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Write round numbers (approximate figures in even units) in words: unit being 100 in numbers <1,000 and 1,000 in numbers >1,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but: 'at 550'); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but: 'of about 2,700'); 'The population of Chicago is approximately two millions' (but: '1,900,000'). For cases like 1,500 spelled out, prefer 'fifteen hundred' rather than 'one thousand five hundred.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. Spell out numbers that commence a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, no matter how high, commencing a sentence in ordinary reading matter should be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women, and 126 children...' When impracticable, reconstruct the sentence to avoid beginning with a numeral: 'The total number of those who went down with the ship was 593 men.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Spell out sums of money in isolated ordinary reading cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated cases in ordinary reading matter should be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The admission was two dollars.' When several such numbers occur close together or in statistical character, use figures: 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Spell out time of day in ordinary reading matter; use figures in statistical/technical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Express time of day in words in ordinary reading matter (e.g., at four; at half-past two in the afternoon; at seven o'clock). Use figures statistically, in enumerations, and always with A.M./P.M.: at 4:15 P.M. (omit 'o'clock' in such contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ordinary prose from technical/statistical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Spell out ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ages in words in ordinary prose: e.g., eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting guidance for ages in narrative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Spell out numbers of centuries, dynasties, sessions, military bodies, thoroughfares, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words for numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, and similar cases, unless brevity is an important consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, second session; Fifteenth Infantry I.N.G.; Sixth Congressional District, Second Ward; Fifth Avenue. (See rules 7, 8, 13 for exceptions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. References to particular decades in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Express references to particular decades in words: e.g., in the nineties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 165 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. Names of months: spell out except in statistical/long enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out names of months in ordinary prose, except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from January 1 to April 15 (omit st, d, and th after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. 'United States' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: 'United States' is generally spelled out except in quotations and specific connections such as military abbreviations, ship names, footnotes, and similar references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where abbreviations are acceptable: General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. 'Oregon'; U.S. Geological Survey. See rules 22, 52, 106.

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. 'Railroad' and geographic 'Fort/Mount/Port' usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'Railroad (-way)' and 'Fort,' 'Mount,' and 'Port' in geographical appellations as words (not abbreviations), with examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad (not: R.R. or Ry.); Fort Wayne, Mount Elias, Port Huron.

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. General rule to spell out names of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, spell out all names of publications. This rule is flexible and may be modified by expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference. When in doubt, spell out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good taste will condone offenses toward spelling out more readily than the opposite. No exhaustive direction provided; apply judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. Abbreviations for U.S. states/territories in bibliographical lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations (without spaces between letters) for names of states, territories, and possessions of the United States when following those of towns in lists, bibliographical matter, etc., but not ordinarily in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (partial list): Ala. Alaska Ariz. Ark. Cal. Colo. Conn. D.C. Del. Fla. Ga. Idaho Ind. Iowa Kan. Ky. La. Me. Md. Mass. Mich. Minn. Miss. Mo. Mont. Neb. Nev. N.H. N.J. N.M. N.Y. N.C. N.D. Ohio Okla. Ore. Pa. P.R. (Porto Rico) R.I. S.C. S.D. Tenn. Tex. Utah Vt. Va. Wash. W.Va. Wis. Wyo. P.I. = Philippine Islands; T.H. = Territory of Hawaii.

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. Abbreviations in technical/bibliographical firm names
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnote references, bibliographies), abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use & (ampersand) in names of commercial firms; in running text not of a technical character, spell these words out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad. In ordinary text: 'Harper Brothers have recently published ...'; 'The Century Company announces ...'. When the commercial name does not consist of proper names, spell out 'and': American Steel and Wire Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' before place names; omit before apostles/evangelists/church fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' before names of places and churches (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church, SS. Peter and Paul), but preferably omit 'St.' when referring to apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine rather than St. Luke, St. Paul).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on ecclesiastical naming conventions and preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Standard abbreviations for books of the Bible, Apocrypha, and common Bible versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standardized abbreviations for books of the Old and New Testaments and the Apocrypha in literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical matter, and use common abbreviations for Bible versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long lists provided for Old Testament (Gen., Exod., Lev., Num., Deut., etc.), New Testament (Matt., Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Rom., etc.), Apocrypha (I and II Esd., Wisd. of Sol., Sus., Tob., Ecclus., etc.). Versions: A.V. = Authorized Version; R.V. = Revised Version; R.V.m. = Revised Version, margin; A.R.V. = American Standard Revised Version; E.R.V. = English Revised Version; Vulg. = Vulgate; LXX = Septuagint.

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. (Implicit) Abbreviations for volume/number/page/figure etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical matter, abbreviate volume, number, psalm, division, chapter, article, section, page, column, verse, line, note, figure, followed by their numbers, and use conventional abbreviations for page ranges and editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I (Vols.), No. 1 (Nos.), Ps. 20 (Pss.), Div. III, chap. ii (chaps.), art. iii (arts.), sec. 4 (secs.), p. 5 (pp.), col. 6 (cols.), vs. 7 (vss.), l. 8 (ll.), n. 9 (nn.), Fig. 7 (Figs.); pp. 5-7 = pages 5 to 7 inclusive; pp. 5 f. = page 5 and the following page; pp. 5 ff. = page 5 and the following pages; ed(d). = edition(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: 111. Abbreviations for U.S. territories/possessions (additional examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide additional shorthand forms for territories/possessions, e.g., N.C., P.R. = Porto Rico, W.Va., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are listed alongside state abbreviations as used in bibliographical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. Use office style for modern extracts; preserve original in Old English or where essential
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling/punctuation differ only slightly from office style, conform to office style; in citations from Old English works or where faithful rendering is essential, follow the original copy. Titles should always be accurately quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply judgement: use office style unless variations are significant to meaning or context. Always accurately quote titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. Forming possessive of proper names ending in s or sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive of proper names ending in s or another sibilant: if monosyllabic, add apostrophe and s; if more than one syllable, add apostrophe only, except names ending in -ce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations, Berlioz' compositions; Horace's odes. For proper names ending in a silent sibilant, form possessive with apostrophe and s regardless of syllable count: Charlevoix's discoveries, Des Moines's population.

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Use 'a' before sounded h, long u (or eu), and the words 'one', 'once'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'a' (not 'an') as the indefinite article before sounded h, long u (or eu), and the words 'one' and 'once'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a harmonic rendition, a historical work, a union, a euphonious word, such a one.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. Do not use ligatures 'ae' and 'oe' at present; retain only in Old English/French
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use ligatures æ and œ in modern English words derived from Latin/Greek; write as ae, oe, or e. Retain ligatures only in Old English and French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aetas; Oedipus Tyrannus; aesthetic; but ceuvre (French). Also exceptions: maneuver; Alfred (in English).

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' to mean 'more remote' or 'at a greater distance'; use 'further' to mean 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.
